implementation_notes: The pattern's canonical Java home is the messaging API itself: the sender creates a Message (ObjectMessage carrying a Serializable command object, or TextMessage carrying JSON/XML) and sends it to a Queue, and the receiver registers a MessageListener whose onMessage extracts the command and invokes the handler. The queue's point-to-point semantics provide the single-receiver contract, and message selectors plus the provider's redelivery settings supply filtering and retry without application code. The classic object-message form is still justified when both sides share one Java runtime and version; across systems or languages, send a text/JSON payload instead.
pitfalls: ObjectMessage binds sender and receiver to the same Java classes and versions (serialVersionUID drift breaks in-flight messages); use a text/JSON payload at any cross-platform boundary.
A session serializes execution of its message listeners: a slow handler stalls that session's other messages unless a container-managed pool is used.
Sending the command to a Topic instead of a Queue turns one command into one execution per subscriber - the single-receiver property is a destination decision, not a message attribute.

variants.name: Spring Cloud Stream functional consumer bound to a destination
variants.implementation_notes: The modern Spring realization declares the receiver as a bean: Spring Cloud Stream binds Consumer<Command> to an inbound destination and invokes it per message, with concurrency, retry, dead-letter and content-type handling configured as binding properties rather than coded. The command stays a plain class or record and the binder is broker-agnostic (Kafka, RabbitMQ, ...), so the point-to-point contract lives in the destination topology. Choose this when the service is Spring-based and the transport should be a configuration decision; choose the JMS form when the provider's API is the contract.
pitfalls: With several Consumer beans and no spring.cloud.function.definition (and autodetection off), the binding target is ambiguous and the app fails to start.

Payload conversion depends on the binder's content type: without a type header a JSON command can arrive as a Map instead of the record, and the failure surfaces as a ClassCastException inside the handler.
Consumer groups decide which instance gets the command; two groups for one command means two executions, exactly like a publish-subscribe channel.
